Hi, and welcome to the A16Z podcast. I'm Lauren Murrow, and in this episode, Patreon co-founder, Sam Yam, and A16C consumer tech partner, Lee Jin, join me to talk about the passion economy.
The rise of online platforms that enable people to make a living off their unique interests and skills.
Though this episode is recorded before the current shelter and place orders, it's a trend that's become increasingly relevant as we see a massive growth in digital work.
Our conversation covers the new forms of work made possible by these online platforms, why creators today are effectively making more money off fewer fans, and what all this means for the future of entrepreneurship.
You can also check out our posts on this topic, as well as related content.
at A16.com slash passion economy.
So first off, how would you define the passion economy?
When I talk about the passion economy, I really mean any potential path of monetization where people
are leveraging their individuality. So it's beyond just podcasters and YouTubers and
and visual content creators. And it encompasses things like video course creators or virtual content creators or
virtual coaches for professional coaching. So some of the really interesting platforms
allow creators to create their own online courses. And these online courses encompass everything from how to

virtual teachers and tutors, there's platforms that are giving people the

creator platforms. In 2013, people were making money online and even online for

few hundred dollars transferred to his back account, right? And if you look at my own life,

reached global scale.

find the creators that they resonated with in order for this next wave of new creator platforms

What types of work would fall under the passion economy umbrella?
In addition to the ones that people

writers, online course creators.

After the Passion Economy blog post came out last fall, I was pleasantly surprised by

I see, so individuality is a feature, not a bug.
But a lot of previous marketplaces were really about providing providing the most consistent experience experience as a

ride button, you knew exactly what to expect.
The difference between that versus passion economy work is that as a consumer,

And so it's not about taking any online course or subscribing to any newsletter.
They're not interchangeable.
Have you noticed a shift in the types of work that you're
seeing on Patreon. Lee has made the analogy that it's like the difference between
Amazon and Shopify, like that standardized mass produced monolith and then the more indie

This is something I want to hone in on.
Is this type of creative work growing?
Is the passion economy or what we would formerly call the creator economy?
Is it growing?

And then all our cohorts are growing over time.

And so I think this speaks to what's going on in the whole industry.

passionate about.
And that's just going to dictate continual growth over time as these children grow up and decide what they want

Another way to think about the total potential market for the passion economy, which, by the way,
was the biggest question that I got after publication of the passion economy

two ways to think about it. One is by looking on all of the different creative platforms like YouTube and Instagram

categories I think could shift to creators and more niche content that individuals
are producing. You mentioned that you got a lot of feedback that was like, this sounds great, but how many

modern digital platforms, in fact, creators need less fans to make a living than they did in the
past. More than decade ago, Kevin Kelly, who is an editor wired, predicted the rise of the
rise of the passion economy. So he basically argued that rather than pursuing, say, widespread
fame, that creators only needed to engage a base of 1,000 true fans. So 1,000 fans that would pay

Kelly's original post, which was that it doesn't take building a huge, massive audience

true fans model. It's a difference in the kind of content they're creating, right?
content and I think the mindset that they're tapping into among their fans.
So the 1,000 true fans model where people are paying you slightly less than $10 a month is really
about tapping into the idea of fan altruism, where users are willing to pay you for something that

In order to get users to pay $1,000 a year,
Obviously, there's a tremendous amount of value that needs to be offered to them in exchange
for that increase in price point. And so the model of 100 true fans is really about the fan benefit

available elsewhere. A lot of it is oriented around delivering tangible value and results.
So, Sam, do you think there's a shift from that influencer model of people subscribing

Well, to the least point, we've certainly seen the average initial pledge amount increase over time
time and also a shift in patrons who are paying over $100 per month, which is over $1,000 a year.
We've seen that grown over the past few years.
I certainly think price point is relevant.
I think to your earlier point, what's being offered is highly relevant to, what's being offered is highly

Okay.

a particular gig, the lovers for growing your revenue was just through

to things that are creator-led.

thesis: The speakers argue that the passion economy represents a shift toward monetizing individuality, where creators leverage unique skills and interests to build communities rather than providing standardized, interchangeable services. This model enables sustainable careers for individuals by allowing them to find specific niches and connect directly with fans, moving away from the broken economics of the past where high engagement did not guarantee viable income.
